metadata.name: Acute bronchitis
metadata.disease_category: Acute self-limiting lower respiratory infection (mostly viral)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine — self-limiting; main task is to exclude pneumonia

overview.short_description: Self-limiting inflammation of the large airways, usually viral, presenting with an acute cough (often productive) in an otherwise well patient without signs of pneumonia.
overview.detailed_description: Acute bronchitis is a common reason for cough presentations. It is predominantly viral and self-limiting; antibiotics provide little benefit in otherwise healthy adults. The central clinical decision is to distinguish it from community-acquired pneumonia (which needs antibiotics) and from asthma/COPD exacerbations, and to avoid unnecessary antibiotics while safety-netting.
overview.pathophysiology: Viral infection of bronchial epithelium causes inflammation, mucus production and airway hyper-responsiveness, producing cough that can persist for weeks after the infection clears.
overview.etiology: Usually respiratory viruses (influenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus, RSV, adenovirus). Bacteria (e.g., Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Bordetella pertussis) are less common causes.
overview.natural_history: Cough is the dominant symptom and commonly lasts up to 3 weeks; most recover fully without specific treatment.
overview.prognosis: Excellent in healthy adults; consider underlying disease if cough persists beyond 3-4 weeks.

prevalence.value: One of the most common acute respiratory presentations in primary care, especially autumn/winter.

incidence.value: Very common; higher in smokers and during viral seasons.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Exposure to respiratory viruses; air pollutants.
risk_factors.smoking: Major risk factor; worsens and prolongs cough and predisposes to COPD.
risk_factors.pregnancy: Not a risk factor; affects medication choice.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Asthma/COPD — presentations may overlap or be exacerbations rather than simple bronchitis.

chief_complaints.complaint: Cough (dry or productive) for days to weeks

chief_complaints.importance: Sputum colour does NOT reliably indicate bacterial infection

symptoms.importance: Colour is not a reliable marker of bacterial infection
Airway hyper-responsiveness; consider asthma if recurrent
High fever should raise concern for pneumonia

symptoms.symptom: Breathlessness at rest / pleuritic pain / high fever
symptoms.importance: RED FLAG — points to pneumonia rather than bronchitis

negative_findings.finding: No focal chest signs (crackles/bronchial breathing), normal saturations, no tachypnoea
negative_findings.why_important: Their absence makes pneumonia much less likely and supports bronchitis without antibiotics

history_questions.question: How long has the cough lasted and is it improving?
history_questions.why_ask: Bronchitis cough can persist ~3 weeks; longer needs review

history_questions.question: Do you have breathlessness at rest, high fever, or pleuritic chest pain?
Any wheeze, recurrent cough, or history of asthma/COPD?
Do you smoke, and are you coughing up blood?
history_questions.why_ask: Smoking risk; haemoptysis needs work-up for other causes

history_questions.question: Any paroxysmal coughing fits with whoop/vomiting?

physical_examination.expected_finding: Usually normal or mildly abnormal; tachypnoea/hypoxia suggests pneumonia
Clear or scattered wheeze/coarse sounds that clear with cough; NO focal crackles/bronchial breathing

vital_signs.respiratory_rate: Normal (tachypnoea is a red flag for pneumonia)
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: >=95% expected; hypoxia is a red flag

laboratory_tests.indication: Not required for typical acute bronchitis
When pneumonia is a possibility and it would guide antibiotic decision
laboratory_tests.expected_result: Low CRP argues against pneumonia/bacterial infection

imaging.when_needed: Suspected pneumonia (focal signs, hypoxia, high fever, or diagnostic uncertainty)
imaging.expected_findings: Normal in bronchitis; consolidation in pneumonia

other_diagnostic_tests.spirometry: Consider after recovery if asthma/COPD suspected (not acutely diagnostic)
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Sputum culture not routine; consider pertussis testing if clinically suspected
other_diagnostic_tests.pcr: Respiratory viral / pertussis PCR only if it changes management

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical diagnosis: acute cough (<3 weeks) with or without sputum, in a patient WITHOUT clinical features of pneumonia (no focal chest signs, no significant tachypnoea/hypoxia/tachycardia, not systemically very unwell).
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: No specific score; CRB-65/CURB-65 assess severity if pneumonia is diagnosed. CRP used to guide antibiotics (NICE).

cutoff_values.value: NICE CRP guidance for lower respiratory infection: <20 mg/L antibiotics not routinely needed; 20-100 delayed antibiotic; >100 offer antibiotics.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Focal chest signs, breathlessness, hypoxia, systemically unwell
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you breathless or is there focal chest pain?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Known airway disease, variable/reversible airflow limitation, recurrent
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have known asthma/COPD or recurrent wheeze?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Paroxysms, inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, weeks-long
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have coughing fits with a whoop or vomiting?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Other causes of chronic cough (if >3-4 weeks): GERD, asthma, ACE inhibitor, lung cancer
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_symptoms: Reflux, ACE inhibitor use, smoking history
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: How long exactly, and any weight loss or coughing blood?

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you breathless at rest or is there focal chest pain, and what are your temperature and breathing like?
diagnostic_questions.purpose: Separate bronchitis from pneumonia (the key decision)
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Focal signs/hypoxia/high fever -> pneumonia; absent -> bronchitis

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have recurrent wheeze or known asthma/COPD?

next_best_question.question: Do you have breathlessness, high fever, or chest pain — and how long has the cough lasted?
next_best_question.expected_answers: No red flags/<3 weeks vs red flags/prolonged
next_best_question.branching_logic: No red flags -> reassure, no antibiotics, safety-net; red flags -> examine chest, consider CXR/CRP and pneumonia pathway

next_best_test.why: When pneumonia is a realistic possibility

red_flags.finding: Breathlessness at rest, tachypnoea, or oxygen saturation <95%
High fever, systemically unwell, confusion, or low blood pressure
Haemoptysis, weight loss, or cough >3 weeks
red_flags.immediate_action: Investigate for other causes (CXR; consider malignancy/TB)

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected pneumonia not manageable in the community; suspected lung cancer (persistent cough/haemoptysis) via urgent pathway.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Persistent or recurrent cough needing spirometry/specialist assessment.

late: Rarely, unmasking of underlying chronic lung disease

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance about the self-limiting course (cough may last ~3 weeks); rest, fluids.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; Antibiotic selected by a clinician. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG120.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net: return if breathless, high fever, coughing blood, or cough persists beyond 3-4 weeks.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Symptomatic: analgesia/antipyretics; honey or over-the-counter cough remedies (limited evidence). ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT ROUTINELY INDICATED; consider only if pneumonia suspected, or in selected high-risk/frail patients per NICE CRP-guided approach. Bronchodilator only if wheeze/airflow obstruction.

patient_education.home_advice: A chest cold (acute bronchitis) is usually caused by a virus. The cough can last up to three weeks even as you recover, and antibiotics usually don't help. Rest, drink fluids, and use paracetamol for aches. See a doctor if you become breathless, have a high fever, cough up blood, or the cough lasts more than three weeks.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب القصبات الحاد (نزلة صدرية) سببه فيروس غالباً. قد يستمر السعال حتى ثلاثة أسابيع حتى مع التحسّن، والمضادات الحيوية عادةً لا تفيد. ارتَح واشرب السوائل وتناول الباراسيتامول للألم. راجع الطبيب إذا صرت تلهث، أو ارتفعت الحرارة، أو خرج دم مع السعال، أو استمرّ السعال أكثر من ثلاثة أسابيع.
patient_education.prevention: Stop smoking, hand hygiene, and consider influenza vaccination.
patient_education.warning_signs: Breathlessness, chest pain, high fever, coughing blood, or cough lasting more than three weeks.

prevention.vaccination: Influenza vaccination reduces some cases; no specific bronchitis vaccine.

evidence.evidence_level: High — evidence shows minimal antibiotic benefit in healthy adults.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG120; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong — NICE, AAFP recommend against routine antibiotics.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Relieve symptoms, exclude pneumonia and avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; Antibiotic selected by a clinician. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG120.
required_history_before_any_medication: age and weight where dosing is weight- or age-dependent
pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances
major cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bleeding history
non_drug_measures: Fluids, rest and safety-net advice; honey may be tried only above 1 year of age.

medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: severe active liver disease or prior serious reaction
use_caution_if: heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, low body weight, or concomitant paracetamol-containing products
monitoring: total daily exposure and clinical response

medication_options.when_to_consider: Pain or fever when suitable after comorbidity review
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: active gastrointestinal bleeding/ulcer, serious NSAID allergy, or NSAID-triggered asthma
use_caution_if: chronic kidney disease, heart failure, hypertension, anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy, older age, pregnancy, or dehydration
monitoring: renal function, blood pressure, oedema and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms when clinically indicated

medication_options.when_to_consider: Systemically very unwell or high complication risk after clinical assessment; not routine
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

use_caution_if: renal impairment, prior C. difficile, or recent antibiotic exposure
monitoring: clinical response, allergy and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea

use_caution_if: liver disease, bradycardia, hypokalaemia, myasthenia gravis, pregnancy, or QT-prolonging medicines
monitoring: clinical response; ECG/electrolytes when risk is material

use_caution_if: oesophageal disease, liver disease, photosensitivity, or interacting iron/calcium/antacid products

procedures_referral_and_escalation: Urgent assessment for hypoxia, sepsis, focal consolidation, haemoptysis or major deterioration.
